source.version_note: Published 20 April 2021; Big Data and Cognitive Computing 5(2):18. The paper attributes the initial DAB concept to the author’s 2018 article, which was not independently fully read here.
source.verification_method: All 14 supplied pages read, including references. Figures 1 and 2 on pages 8–9 rendered and visually inspected because extracted text is duplicated and omits diagram labels. Crossref verifies main identity and selected reference metadata. A selected passage of the Deep Learning book introduction was checked for learning-paradigm terminology; the full book and cited original bias taxonomy were not read.

citation.title: Deep Automation Bias: How to Tackle a Wicked Problem of AI?

reading.source_scope_note: Conceptual technology-assessment argument and draft review heuristic. No new participant study, benchmark, causal estimate or tested oversight intervention. DAB is a proposed systemic risk framing; Friedman–Nissenbaum bias classes and other empirical examples are secondary citations.
access_limits: Complete supplied article and both diagrams read. No raw data or empirical study is provided. Cited original studies, books, reports, legal frameworks and investigative journalism were not independently fully read.

Bibliographic corrections use metadata; the deep-learning correction uses a selected primary textbook passage, not a complete book review. The hypothetical autonomous autopilot is not a verified deployed aircraft system.

study.type: Non-systematic conceptual synthesis from technology assessment and science-and-technology studies. No sampling, preregistered protocol, quantitative risk model or measured outcomes.
study.bias_taxonomy: Secondary summary of Friedman and Nissenbaum (1996): pre-existing social bias, design/functionality-related technical bias and emergent bias from mismatch with a deployment context. Context dependence can concern practices and institutional requirements, not just a changed statistical input distribution.
study.systemic_proposal: DAB combines overreliance/misinterpretation with limited controllability/agency. Proposed feedback links opaque, complex system behavior, users’ skills/resources/awareness and inadequate scrutiny or intervention. Dependence and lack of alternatives may reinforce acceptance of insufficient functionality. These are conceptual relationships, not fitted effects or inevitable outcomes.
study.figure_one: Figure 1 pairs usability with skills, model/data quality with resources/practical experience, and accountability/scrutiny with problem awareness. Uncertainty connects the technical and user circles, between overreliance at the top and limited control at the bottom. No numeric scale, weights, thresholds or validation is supplied.
study.review_heuristic: Figure 2 and section 6 propose recurring human review of input, output and action: explicability/comprehensibility, validity, plausibility/traceability, then contextual legal/ethical acceptability. Doubts trigger expert review; compliance questions lead to proposed suspension pending review. Multidisciplinary boards and periodic in-depth reviews are proposed even without visible irregularities. These recommendations are not automatically adopted as a universal shutdown policy.
study.assurance_boundary: Passing the four queries means no issue was observed during that review; it cannot establish absence of hidden bias, lawful deployment, universal safety or complete causal explanation. A human-in-the-loop label does not guarantee usable time, skill, information or intervention authority.
study.technical_scope: The supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement/deep-learning list mixes learning settings with a family of representations. It does not establish an autonomy ranking. Training/adaptation, runtime control, opacity and operational authority require separate specification. Broad claims that AI cannot adapt and adaptation necessarily worsens risk remain untested generalizations.
study.wicked_problems: The Rittel–Webber planning framework highlights disputed values and interdependent consequences. The author explicitly cautions that not all ten properties apply to technical AI. These properties do not prohibit experimentation, create literally untestable software or authorize unlimited work without stopping rules.
study.examples: Hiring-background discrimination and clinical overreliance are secondary accounts. A permanently self-optimizing, non-overridable autopilot is an imagined illustration, not an original empirical finding or established aviation architecture.

summary: Add deep automation bias as an explicitly proposed systemic risk and emergent bias as contextual unfairness, not duplicate names for ordinary automation bias. Enrich automation bias, solutionism and agency laundering. Keep the draft oversight framework and technical claims qualified.

findings.definition: A proposed systemic risk in which opaque automation, mismatches with user practices and inadequate scrutiny or intervention reinforce overreliance and dependence on the system.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Author’s conceptual metarisk framing, extending an earlier 2018 proposal; no new measured effect, validated risk score or inevitable consequence of AI.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate system–workflow mismatches together with error acceptance, users’ ability to detect/correct outputs, real intervention authority and availability of alternatives. Track whether reliance persists after limitations are disclosed. Separate prediction error from institutional incentives and control constraints.
findings.novelty_rationale: Ordinary automation bias concerns unwarranted reliance on a machine output. This proposed framework additionally concerns systemic feedback, workflow mismatch, blocked scrutiny/intervention and dependence. Preserve that broader unit of analysis rather than use deep as a synonym for stronger individual bias.

evidence.quote: DAB is thus a metarisk of AI systems and their intrinsic dynamics.
conflicts or undetected mismatches between the behavior of an AI system and human user practices

findings.evidence_scope: Sections 5–7 and both diagrams elaborate a conceptual account. The paper names technical and organizational contributors and proposes regular/in-depth review. It supplies no comparative prevalence, causal validation or evidence that all deep models self-modify at runtime.
findings.boundary: Complexity, automation or uncertainty alone does not demonstrate DAB. Evidence should connect actual contextual mismatch to unjustified reliance, impaired scrutiny/control or reinforcing dependence. Deep learning is neither required for every automation failure nor a synonym for online self-modification.

findings.definition: Unfair disadvantage arising when a system’s design or assumptions fail to fit the people, practices or requirements of its deployment context.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary conceptual account of Friedman and Nissenbaum’s taxonomy; no new prevalence estimate, comparison or independent reading of the 1996 original.
findings.ai_proposal: Review new populations, workflows and institutional requirements before reuse. Compare consequential errors and access burdens across affected groups, including changed practices without statistical input drift. Preserve deployment context and responsible reviewer records.
findings.novelty_rationale: Bias migration concerns the location/source of error after assistance, while value misgeneralisation concerns a learned proxy applied off-distribution. Emergent bias concerns contextual fit and unfair disadvantage in use, including unchanged models and non-learning systems. Context collapse concerns conversational audience mixing instead.

evidence.quote: can lead to discrimination of individuals or groups
some kind of mismatch between what users or a usage context requires, and what the system features

findings.evidence_scope: Pages 2–3 summarize a three-part historical taxonomy and illustrate context mismatch with hospital resource allocation reused in a rural clinic. This is a secondary illustrative example, not an evaluated hospital deployment or evidence of a particular harmed group.
findings.boundary: Not every domain change, inaccurate output or distribution shift is unfair bias. Identify relevant contextual requirements, affected people and unjustified disadvantage. A system can be contextually inappropriate without a measured change in its input distribution; causal data and normative criteria still need case-specific evidence.

findings.definition: Trusting a tool result or a prior step because a machine produced it, without verifying the load-bearing part.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source directly discusses uncritical acceptance and distinguishes that individual reliance tendency from its broader DAB framework.

evidence.quote: the tendency to uncritically accept the computer-generated outcome

findings.evidence_scope: Narrative synthesis cites earlier empirical automation research for inexperience, low confidence, inadequate checking options and workload/time constraints. These are not new effect estimates or independently reviewed experiments here.
findings.boundary: Appropriate reliance on demonstrably reliable automation is not bias. Show unwarranted acceptance relative to available evidence and feasible verification, and distinguish lack of attention from acceptance after noticing conflicting evidence.

findings.definition: Treating complex social problems as solvable by technology.
findings.novelty_rationale: The critique directly addresses the existing concept; no new label for techno-fixes is needed.

evidence.quote: societal problems cannot be fixed by technological means only
it would only be a one-shot solution to a symptom of a larger (wicked) problem

findings.evidence_scope: The paper argues that narrowly removing a biased feature may leave other institutional/design causes unresolved. This is a conceptual critique of technical sufficiency, while the author also acknowledges relevant technical debiasing work.
findings.boundary: Technical mitigation can be necessary and effective for specific defects. Neither this critique nor a wicked-problem label proves all technical fixes futile or excuses failing to correct a known defect.

findings.definition: Obscuring a human actor’s role in morally suspect actions by attributing those actions to an algorithm, machine or technical system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Explicit secondary discussion maps to the existing responsibility-evasion concept, not a separate ethics-laundering entry.

evidence.quote: misused to avoid taking responsibility by reframing the problems to sheer technical issues

findings.evidence_scope: The conclusion cites Tsamados et al. and argues that technical reframing may leave ethical problems and human responsibility unaddressed. No laundering prevalence or specific organizational intent is measured.
findings.boundary: Using a technical explanation, conducting debiasing or sharing responsibility is not laundering by itself. Identify the obscured human decision/duty and how attribution to the system impedes justified accountability.

source_corrections.location: Page 5 machine-learning autonomy hierarchy and Figure 2 list
source_corrections.issue: Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement and deep learning are listed as if mutually exclusive types with an increasing degree of automation; deep learning is assigned the highest automation/self-optimization.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Deep learning can use supervised or unsupervised learning, and can be combined with reinforcement learning. These labels do not alone determine runtime autonomy, continuous updating or override authority. Figure 2’s list should be treated as overlapping descriptions, not a taxonomy establishing control level.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Selected introductory passage on supervised and unsupervised deep models read; no full book reading, aircraft-system validation or universal empirical autonomy ranking.

source_corrections.issue: Rittel’s coauthor is called Marvin Webber.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The coauthor is Melvin M. Webber. Rittel and Webber (1973), Policy Sciences 4(2):155–169, DOI 10.1007/BF01405730. The broader origin/history assertion was not independently resolved.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Author/title/locator metadata only; not a full original-paper or historical-origin review.

source_corrections.issue: Obermeyer et al. (2019) is listed as Science volume 336.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The final article is Science 366(6464):447–453, DOI 10.1126/science.aax2342.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Metadata identity/locators checked; no independent full reading or reproduction of the original study.

methodological_limits: The proposed feedback structure and heuristic are not empirically validated. No relative risk, intervention effect, score weights or sensitivity/specificity can be extracted.
Explicability, formal validity, plausibility and ethical acceptability are distinct. Passing a checklist cannot certify their completeness or guarantee justified outcomes.
Opacity and adaptivity are contingent system properties, not universal laws of AI; runtime updating, learning setting and operational authority differ.
No single debiasing technique can be declared universally sufficient or useless from these conceptual examples.
The hospital, hiring and aviation examples remain secondary or hypothetical; no actual deployment audit was performed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Both require usable scrutiny and control across technical/human contributions. A system-level risk framing complements the problem of many things and human answerability; complexity alone does not eliminate responsible duties.

Never-skilling concerns failure to acquire skills, whereas DAB concerns wider reliance/control feedback. Expert review must have actual capacity and authority; naming a responsible human does not create meaningful oversight.

deferred.reason: A planning framework and its properties, not ten separate behaviors. Retain contextual/value-conflict lessons in the review without importing no-stopping/no-tests language as operational instructions.
Broad causal-source categories overlapping many existing social/data/design mechanisms. Preserve taxonomy in the review; do not multiply broad buckets without a distinct operational boundary.

deferred.term: Four-stage DAB review / critical AI literacy
deferred.reason: Proposed assessment and education approaches, not independent demonstrated behavioral effects or validated safeguards.
Used here for deployment mismatch closely overlapping emergent bias. Preserve the narrower context distinction in that entry rather than add an ambiguous synonym spanning unrelated context effects.

limitations: Cited books and primary studies remain secondary. Do not count the author’s 2018 precursor as an additional full read or the draft heuristic as a validated intervention. No bibliometric time series or automatic ethical/harm edges are added.
